subject: chemistry

items.q: Which statement about the nucleus of an atom is correct?
items.correct: Its density is far greater than the average density of the atom.
items.misconception: It takes up most of the atom's volume, with electrons at its surface.
items.why: Textbook diagrams cannot draw an atom to scale: the nucleus is drawn as a large central ball with electron shells close around it, and students take the picture as a scale drawing. Nearly all the volume of an atom is the space occupied by the electrons. The nucleus is of order 10⁻¹⁵ m across and the atom of order 10⁻¹⁰ m, so the nucleus is a dense, positively charged speck at the centre.
items.specStatementText: Atoms contain a positively charged, dense nucleus composed of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Negatively charged electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
items.random_wrong: It contains only about two-thirds of the mass of the atom.

items.q: Which statement about the relative masses and relative charges of subatomic particles is correct?
items.correct: A proton and an electron carry charges that are equal in size.
items.misconception: A proton carries a larger charge than an electron does.
items.why: Mass and charge are both 'amounts' that a particle carries and are easily conflated, and diagrams that show a large nucleus and tiny electrons suggest that the bigger particle is 'stronger'. Students who already believe that the nucleus pulls on electrons more strongly than electrons pull on the nucleus may attribute this to a larger charge on the heavier particle. The relative charge of a proton is +1 and that of an electron is −1: equal in size. This is why a neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons. The electron's mass is about 1/1836 of the proton's, but its charge is just as large.
items.specStatementText: Atoms contain a positively charged, dense nucleus composed of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Negatively charged electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
items.random_wrong: A neutron carries a charge opposite in sign to a proton's.

items.q: An atom of sodium, ²³₁₁Na (mass number 23, atomic number 11), forms the ion Na⁺. How does the mass of the ion compare with the mass of the atom?
items.correct: It is smaller by a negligible amount, because one electron was lost.
items.misconception: It is larger by a negligible amount, because one electron has been gained.
items.why: In everyday language 'positive' and 'plus' mean gaining or adding something, and 'negative' and 'minus' mean losing. Students map the sign of the charge onto the direction of electron change, forgetting that the electron is itself the negatively charged particle. Electrons carry negative charge. Losing electrons leaves more protons than electrons, so the ion is positive; gaining electrons gives more electrons than protons, so the ion is negative. S²⁻ (Z = 16) has 16 + 2 = 18 electrons.
items.specStatementText: Atoms contain a positively charged, dense nucleus composed of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Negatively charged electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
items.random_wrong: It is larger by about one unit, because the ion has gained one proton.

items.q: How many electrons are there in one ³³₁₆S²⁻ ion (mass number 33, atomic number 16, charge 2−)?
items.why:
A − Z is the only subtraction taught with the nuclear symbol, and the three particle counts are often memorised as a list of rules. Without the reason behind the rule (A counts nucleons, and electrons are not nucleons), it is easily attached to the wrong particle. A counts the protons and neutrons in the nucleus; electrons are outside the nucleus and are not counted in A. Neutrons = A − Z. Electrons = Z in a neutral atom, and Z − (charge) in an ion.

Working: Protons = Z = 16. Electrons = Z − (charge) = 16 − (−2) = 18. (Neutrons = A − Z = 33 − 16 = 17.)
items.specStatementText: Atoms contain a positively charged, dense nucleus composed of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Negatively charged electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
items.working: Protons = Z = 16. Electrons = Z − (charge) = 16 − (−2) = 18. (Neutrons = A − Z = 33 − 16 = 17.)

items.q: An ion X³⁺ contains 23 electrons and 30 neutrons. Which nuclear symbol represents this ion? (Each symbol is written with its superscript first and its subscript second.)
items.correct: ⁵⁶₂₆X³⁺
items.misconception: ⁵³₂₃X³⁺
items.why:
The rule 'number of electrons = atomic number' is learned first, for atoms, and then applied to every particle. The charge written on the symbol is treated as a separate label rather than as a record of electrons lost or gained. The charge on an ion is the difference between its numbers of protons and electrons. An ion with charge 3+ has three electrons fewer than protons; an ion with charge 2− has two more electrons than protons.

Working: Charge = protons − electrons, so protons = 23 + 3 = 26 = Z. A = protons + neutrons = 26 + 30 = 56. Symbol ⁵⁶₂₆X³⁺ (the element is iron).
items.specStatementText: Atoms contain a positively charged, dense nucleus composed of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Negatively charged electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
items.working: Charge = protons − electrons, so protons = 23 + 3 = 26 = Z. A = protons + neutrons = 26 + 30 = 56. Symbol ⁵⁶₂₆X³⁺ (the element is iron).

items.q: Two atoms have the same atomic number but different mass numbers. Which statement about these atoms is correct?
items.correct: They belong to the same element, as they differ only in their numbers of neutrons.
items.misconception: They belong to different elements, as they contain different numbers of nucleons in total.
items.why: Periodic tables list a mass for every element and elements are often described informally as ordered by 'weight', so students identify an element by its mass. The atomic number is seen as a position number rather than as the defining property. What makes an atom an atom of a particular element is its number of protons. Isotopes have the same number of protons and differ only in the number of neutrons, so they are the same element.
items.specStatementText: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
items.random_wrong: They have different numbers of electrons, as their mass numbers are different.

items.q: Chlorine (atomic number 17) has isotopes with mass numbers 35 and 37. Pure samples of ³⁵Cl₂ gas and ³⁷Cl₂ gas are compared at the same temperature and pressure. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: The ³⁷Cl₂ gas diffuses more slowly than ³⁵Cl₂.
items.misconception: The two gases diffuse at the same rate as each other.
items.why: The rule 'isotopes have the same chemical properties' is over-extended to 'isotopes have the same properties', and 'the same element' is taken to mean 'the same substance in every respect'. Isotopes differ in mass. At the same temperature, heavier particles move more slowly, so a gas of the heavier isotope diffuses more slowly and is denser at the same pressure, and compounds of different isotopes have slightly different melting and boiling points.
items.specStatementText: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
items.random_wrong: The two gases undergo different chemical reactions.

items.q: Hydrogen (atomic number 1) has isotopes ¹H and ²H. Water made from ²H, D₂O, melts at 3.8 °C, boils at 101.4 °C and has a density of about 1.1 g cm⁻³; ordinary water, H₂O, melts at 0.0 °C, boils at 100.0 °C and has a density of about 1.0 g cm⁻³. Both react with sodium in the same way: H₂O forms NaOH and H₂, and D₂O forms NaOD and D₂. Which statement accounts for these observations?
items.correct: D₂O molecules are heavier than H₂O molecules, but have the same electron arrangement.
items.misconception: D₂O molecules contain more electrons, so the forces between them are stronger.
items.why: Isotopes and ions are both introduced as 'different versions of an atom', often in the same lesson, and students do not keep separate which particle changes in each case. A change in the number of electrons makes an ion; a change in the number of neutrons makes a different isotope. ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl atoms both have 17 electrons; they differ by two neutrons.
items.specStatementText: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
items.random_wrong: Boiling D₂O breaks its O–D bonds, which need more energy to break than O–H bonds.

items.q: A sample of chlorine contains 75.8% chlorine-35 (relative isotopic mass 34.97) and 24.2% chlorine-37 (relative isotopic mass 36.97). What is the relative atomic mass of chlorine in this sample?
items.why:
The everyday meaning of 'average' is 'add them up and divide by how many', and this procedure is applied without asking how many atoms of each isotope there are. A_r = Σ(relative isotopic mass × percentage abundance) ÷ 100. An abundant isotope pulls A_r toward its own mass; for two isotopes, A_r lies closer to the more abundant one.

Working: A_r = Σ(relative isotopic mass × % abundance) ÷ 100 = (75.8 × 34.97 + 24.2 × 36.97) ÷ 100 = (2650.73 + 894.67) ÷ 100 = 3545.40 ÷ 100 = 35.45 (no units).
items.specStatementText: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.

items.q: Copper has two isotopes, copper-63 and copper-65, with relative isotopic masses 62.93 and 64.93. The relative atomic mass of copper is 63.55. What is the percentage abundance of copper-65?
items.why:
Each difference is formed from one isotope's mass, so it looks as if it 'belongs' to that isotope. Students do not check the answer against the idea that A_r lies closer to the more abundant isotope. Write x for the fraction of one isotope and (1 − x) for the other, and solve. Then check: the isotope whose mass is closer to A_r must be the more abundant one.

Working: Let the abundance of copper-65 be x%. Then 64.93x + 62.93(100 − x) = 63.55 × 100 → 6293 + 2.00x = 6355 → x = 62 ÷ 2.00 = 31.0%. (Copper-63: 69.0%.)
items.specStatementText: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.

items.q: The mass spectrum of element E shows three peaks from singly charged atomic ions: m/z 24 (relative abundance 100), m/z 25 (relative abundance 12.7) and m/z 26 (relative abundance 13.9). What is the relative atomic mass of E, calculated from these data?
items.why:
In A_r calculations from percentage data students always divide by 100, and a peak height of 100 looks like '100%'. The scaling of the tallest peak to 100 is not noticed. Add up the relative abundances first. If the tallest peak is 100, the total is more than 100; divide the weighted sum by that total. A check: A_r must lie between the smallest and largest m/z values.

Working: Σ(relative abundance) = 100 + 12.7 + 13.9 = 126.6. Σ(m/z × relative abundance) = 2400 + 317.5 + 361.4 = 3078.9. A_r = 3078.9 ÷ 126.6 = 24.32 (no units).
items.specStatementText: Mass spectra are used to determine the relative atomic masses of elements from their isotopic composition.

items.q: The mass spectrum of element X, showing only the peaks from singly charged atomic ions (X⁺), has two peaks: m/z 79 (relative abundance 100) and m/z 81 (relative abundance 97.3). Atomic numbers: selenium 34, bromine 35, gadolinium 64, gold 79. Which element is X?
items.correct: Element X is bromine (A_r 79.90).
items.misconception: Element X is selenium (A_r 78.97).
items.why:
The tallest peak is the most eye-catching feature of the spectrum, and in spectra of molecules students are told to look for one particular peak; they carry over the idea that one peak gives 'the answer'. Every peak contributes. A_r = Σ(m/z × relative abundance) ÷ Σ(relative abundances), so it lies between the smallest and largest m/z values and is pulled toward the tallest peak.

Working: Σ(relative abundance) = 100 + 97.3 = 197.3. A_r = (79 × 100 + 81 × 97.3) ÷ 197.3 = (7900 + 7881.3) ÷ 197.3 = 79.99 → closest to bromine (A_r 79.90). (m/z values are whole numbers here, so the calculated value differs slightly from the accepted A_r.)
items.specStatementText: Mass spectra are used to determine the relative atomic masses of elements from their isotopic composition.
items.working: Σ(relative abundance) = 100 + 97.3 = 197.3. A_r = (79 × 100 + 81 × 97.3) ÷ 197.3 = (7900 + 7881.3) ÷ 197.3 = 79.99 → closest to bromine (A_r 79.90). (m/z values are whole numbers here, so the calculated value differs slightly from the accepted A_r.)

items.q: The mass spectrum of a sample of copper shows two peaks from singly charged atomic ions: m/z 63 (relative abundance 100) and m/z 65 (relative abundance 44.6). What do these peaks show?
items.correct: Copper atoms exist with two numbers of neutrons, 34 and 36.
items.misconception: The sample also contains a second element, of mass 65.
items.why: Periodic tables list a mass for every element and elements are often described informally as ordered by 'weight', so students identify an element by its mass. The atomic number is seen as a position number rather than as the defining property. What makes an atom an atom of a particular element is its number of protons. Isotopes have the same number of protons and differ only in the number of neutrons, so they are the same element.
items.specStatementText: Mass spectra are used to determine the relative atomic masses of elements from their isotopic composition.
items.random_wrong: The A_r of copper is 63, which is the m/z of the tallest peak.

items.q: How many neutrons are there in one atom of ⁸¹₃₅Br (mass number 81, atomic number 35)?
items.why:
The first atoms students meet, such as ⁴He, ¹²C and ¹⁶O, happen to have equal numbers of all three particles, so the pattern is generalised to every atom. Only the numbers of protons and electrons are linked (they are equal in a neutral atom). The number of neutrons must be worked out as A − Z: ⁸¹₃₅Br has 35 protons, 35 electrons and 81 − 35 = 46 neutrons.

Working: Protons = Z = 35. Mass number A = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = A − Z = 81 − 35 = 46.
items.specStatementText: Atoms contain a positively charged, dense nucleus composed of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Negatively charged electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
items.working: Protons = Z = 35. Mass number A = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = A − Z = 81 − 35 = 46.

items.q: Does forming an ion change the number of protons in the nucleus?
items.correct: No. Ions form by the loss or gain of electrons. The number of protons (and neutrons) is unchanged, so the atomic number and the element stay the same.
items.misconception: A positive ion has gained protons (and a negative ion has lost protons): the charge on an ion comes from a change in the number of protons.
items.why: Protons are 'the positive particles', so a positive charge is read as 'extra protons'. Students do not connect this with the fact that changing the number of protons would change the element. This idea is widely reported in chemistry-education research on students' models of ions. Only electrons are transferred when ions form. Na⁺ has the same 11 protons as a sodium atom and one electron fewer; Cl⁻ has the same 17 protons as a chlorine atom and one electron more.
items.specStatementText: Atoms contain a positively charged, dense nucleus composed of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Negatively charged electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In the nuclear symbol ᴬ_Z X, which number is the atomic number?
items.correct: The subscript Z is the atomic number (number of protons); the superscript A is the mass number (protons + neutrons). A is never smaller than Z.
items.misconception: Mass number and atomic number are confused: in ᴬ_Z X the upper number is taken as the atomic number, and in general a mass value (a mass number or an m/z value) is read as the atomic number.
items.why: Many periodic tables print the atomic number at the top of each element's box and the relative atomic mass below it, which is the opposite of the nuclear symbol. Both are simply 'the numbers next to the symbol', so the periodic-table layout is transferred to the nuclear symbol. Both are whole numbers attached to an element, and the atomic number is the number students have learned identifies an element, so any prominent whole number is read as Z. In ᴬ_Z X the mass number is the superscript and the atomic number is the subscript. A check: the mass number counts protons and neutrons, so it is the larger number (or equal, for ¹₁H).
items.specStatementText: Atoms contain a positively charged, dense nucleus composed of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Negatively charged electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do electrons make a significant contribution to the mass of an atom?
items.correct: No. An electron's relative mass is about 0.0005 (about 1/1836 of a proton's mass), so its mass can be considered negligible. Nearly all the mass of an atom is in the nucleus.
items.misconception: An electron has a mass similar to that of a proton, so electrons make up a significant part of an atom's mass, and gaining or losing an electron changes the mass by about one unit.
items.why: Protons, neutrons and electrons are introduced together as 'the three subatomic particles' and are drawn as dots of similar size in atomic diagrams, so students assume they have similar masses. The tiny mass of the electron is rarely emphasised. Relative masses: proton 1, neutron 1, electron about 0.0005. Losing or gaining an electron changes the mass of a particle by a negligible amount, and the mass number counts only protons and neutrons.
items.specStatementText: Atoms contain a positively charged, dense nucleus composed of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Negatively charged electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: What is the charge of a neutron?
items.correct: Zero. The neutron has relative charge 0. An atom is neutral because its number of electrons equals its number of protons.
items.misconception: Neutrons carry a negative charge that balances the positive charge of the protons, which is why the nucleus (or the atom) is neutral.
items.why: The name 'neutron' suggests something that neutralises, and students look for a partner inside the nucleus to cancel the protons' charge. They do not yet see that the balancing negative charge is carried by the electrons outside the nucleus. Neutrons have no charge. The nucleus is positive, with a relative charge equal to the number of protons. The atom as a whole is neutral because the electrons outside the nucleus carry an equal negative charge.
items.specStatementText: Atoms contain a positively charged, dense nucleus composed of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Negatively charged electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Where are the electrons in an atom?
items.correct: Outside the nucleus. The nucleus contains only protons and neutrons; the electrons occupy the space around it.
items.misconception: Electrons are inside the nucleus, together with the protons and neutrons.
items.why: Students who have met the 'plum pudding' model, in which electrons are embedded in positive matter, or who picture the atom as one solid ball, place all its particles together. The word 'nucleus' is also used loosely to mean 'the core, where everything is'. The nucleus is made of nucleons only: protons and neutrons. Electrons occupy the much larger space outside the nucleus, which is why almost all the volume of an atom contains no nucleus at all.
items.specStatementText: Atoms contain a positively charged, dense nucleus composed of protons and neutrons (nucleons). Negatively charged electrons occupy the space outside the nucleus.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do isotopes of an element have different chemical properties?
items.correct: No. Chemical reactions involve electrons, and isotopes have the same number and arrangement of electrons, so they undergo the same chemical reactions.
items.misconception: Isotopes of an element have different chemical properties, because their atoms have different masses (and some isotopes are radioactive).
items.why: Isotopes are often first met through radioactivity, and students assume that any difference between atoms must change how they react. The link between chemical properties and electron arrangement is not yet secure. Chemical properties depend on the electrons. Isotopes have identical electron arrangements, so ³⁵Cl and ³⁷Cl, or ¹H and ²H, form the same compounds in the same reactions. Only properties that depend on mass differ.
items.specStatementText: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the relative atomic mass equal to the mass of the most abundant isotope?
items.correct: No. A_r is the abundance-weighted mean of all the isotopes, so it is pulled away from the most abundant isotope's mass toward the other isotopes.
items.misconception: The relative atomic mass of an element is the mass of its most abundant isotope; the other isotopes are too rare to count.
items.why: Students meet A_r values that are close to whole numbers (C 12.01, O 16.00) and conclude that A_r is simply the mass of the common isotope. The weighting by abundance is seen as a small correction that can be ignored. Every isotope contributes in proportion to its abundance. Chlorine-37 makes up about a quarter of chlorine atoms, which raises A_r from 34.97 to 35.45.
items.specStatementText: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: After weighting each isotopic mass by its fractional abundance, is the total divided by the number of isotopes?
items.correct: No. Σ(relative isotopic mass × fractional abundance) is already the weighted mean. Dividing again by the number of isotopes is wrong.
items.misconception: After each isotopic mass has been multiplied by its fractional abundance, the total must still be divided by the number of isotopes, as in an ordinary mean.
items.why: The ordinary-mean procedure ('add and divide by how many') is layered on top of the weighted-mean procedure, because students recognise both as 'finding an average' and apply both. The fractional abundances add up to 1, so the weighted sum is already the mean. A check: A_r must lie between the lightest and heaviest isotopic masses; a value far below them shows an extra division.
items.specStatementText: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In a reverse calculation, can the abundances of both isotopes be written as the same unknown x?
items.correct: No. The abundances add up to 100%, so if one isotope has abundance x%, the other has (100 − x)%.
items.misconception: When the abundances are unknown, each isotope's abundance can be written as x, without using the fact that the abundances add up to 100%.
items.why: Students learn to 'let x be the unknown' and write it wherever an abundance is missing, without recognising that the two abundances are linked by the total of 100%. For two isotopes: m₁x + m₂(100 − x) = 100 × A_r. Only one unknown is needed because the second abundance is fixed by the first.
items.specStatementText: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are covalent bonds broken when a molecular substance such as water boils?
items.correct: No. Boiling a molecular substance overcomes the intermolecular forces between its molecules; the O–H (or O–D) bonds inside the molecules are not broken.
items.misconception: When a covalent substance boils, its covalent bonds break, so a higher boiling point means stronger covalent bonds.
items.why: Boiling is described as "breaking apart" the liquid, and students do not separate bonds within molecules from forces between molecules; this is one of the most widely reported misconceptions about covalent substances in chemistry-education research. When water boils, whole H₂O molecules leave the liquid and the steam is still H₂O. What is overcome is the attraction between molecules, not the covalent bonds within them, so a difference in boiling point between two molecular substances is not evidence about the strength of their covalent bonds.
items.specStatementText: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: In an A_r calculation, can the mass numbers of the isotopes be used when their relative isotopic masses are given?
items.correct: Use the relative isotopic masses given; they differ slightly from the mass numbers, and in a reverse calculation the difference changes the answer.
items.misconception: The mass numbers of the isotopes can be used in place of their relative isotopic masses in A_r calculations.
items.why: GCSE A_r calculations use whole-number mass numbers (35, 37), and the isotope names (copper-63, copper-65) display them, so students take them as the masses even when isotopic masses are given. The mass number is a count of nucleons; the relative isotopic mass is a measured mass relative to one-twelfth of a carbon-12 atom. When relative isotopic masses are given, use them: for copper, (63.55 − 62.93) ÷ (64.93 − 62.93) = 0.310, whereas the mass numbers give (63.55 − 63) ÷ (65 − 63) = 0.275.
items.specStatementText: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here, and no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is the mass number the number of neutrons in an atom?
items.correct: No. The mass number A is the total number of protons and neutrons (nucleons). The number of neutrons is A − Z.
items.misconception: The mass number is the number of neutrons in the nucleus.
items.why: The mass number is introduced alongside the number of neutrons, and neutrons are thought of as the particles that add mass without charge, so 'mass number' and 'neutron number' are merged. A counts every nucleon: protons and neutrons. Subtract the atomic number to get the neutrons: neutrons = A − Z.
